title: How to Identify a Thread from Diameter and Pitch
summary: Step-by-step thread identification from diameter and pitch measurements. Tools, technique, cross-reference tables for NPT, BSP, and Metric threads.
body_markdown:
Measure the major diameter with calipers (0.01mm resolution), measure the pitch with a thread gauge (TPI for inch, mm for metric), check for taper, then cross-reference the three values against a thread table. The combination of diameter + pitch + taper/parallel uniquely identifies the thread standard.


## When measurement is the only option


Thread markings wear off. Packaging gets separated from fittings. Suppliers ship products with vague descriptions like "1/2 inch thread" without specifying the standard. When the only reliable data source is the physical fitting, you need to measure.


This guide covers the tools, technique, and cross-reference process for identifying a thread from physical measurements.


## Tools you need


**Digital calipers** with 0.01mm (0.0005") resolution. Dial calipers work but digital is faster. You need to measure outside diameters to sub-millimetre accuracy because the difference between NPT and BSP at the same nominal size can be less than 0.5mm.


**Thread pitch gauge** (also called a screw pitch gauge or thread comb). A set of thin metal blades, each cut with a specific pitch. You hold each blade against the thread until one matches perfectly. Get a set that covers both metric pitches (0.5mm to 6mm) and inch pitches (8 TPI to 32 TPI).


**Taper gauge or straight edge.** A steel ruler or precision straight edge to check whether the thread tapers. Alternatively, take two diameter measurements at different points.


**Thread identification reference.** A printed table, a reference card, or the[thread cross-reference tool](https://www.rastro.ai/tools/thread-cross-reference) for looking up your measurements.


## Step 1: Measure the major diameter


The major diameter is the outside diameter of a male thread (the largest diameter) or the inside diameter of a female thread (the smallest diameter at the thread crests).


**For male threads:** Close the caliper jaws over the thread at the first fully formed thread. Not at the chamfered entry. Not at the end where threads may be incomplete. Measure perpendicular to the thread axis.


**For female threads:** Measure the minor diameter (bore) and add the thread depth to estimate major diameter. Or measure directly at the crest of the internal thread if your calipers can reach.


**For tapered threads:** Measure at the gauge plane (the point where a standard gauge ring would sit). In practice, measure at the fourth or fifth full thread from the end. This is where the thread dimension matches the nominal specification.


Record the diameter in millimetres. Even for inch threads, measuring in millimetres gives you more precision for cross-referencing.


Common major diameters for pipe threads:


Nominal size NPT OD (mm) BSP OD (mm) Difference


1/4" 13.72 13.16 0.56mm


3/8" 17.15 16.66 0.49mm


1/2" 21.34 20.95 0.39mm


3/4" 26.67 26.44 0.23mm


1" 33.40 33.25 0.15mm


At 1" nominal, the difference between NPT and BSP is only 0.15mm. Caliper accuracy matters.


## Step 2: Measure the pitch


**For suspected inch threads (NPT, BSP):** Use an inch thread pitch gauge. Hold each blade flat against the thread and look for light between the blade and thread crests. When no light passes, the blade matches. Read the TPI from the blade. Common TPI values for pipe threads: 8, 11, 11.5, 14, 18, 19, 27, 28.


**For suspected metric threads:** Use a metric thread pitch gauge. Same technique. Read the pitch in millimetres. Common metric pitches: 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0mm.


**If you do not have a gauge:** Measure the distance across 10 thread crests with calipers, then divide by 9 (the number of gaps between 10 crests). This gives you the pitch in millimetres. For TPI, divide 25.4 by the pitch in mm.


NPT and BSP sometimes share the same TPI at the same nominal size. For example, both 1/2" NPT and 1/2" BSP have 14 TPI. In these cases, the pitch alone does not distinguish them. You need the diameter.


## Step 3: Check for taper


**Method 1: Straight edge.** Hold a straight edge along the thread parallel to the axis. On a tapered thread, you will see a gap that increases toward the end of the fitting. On a parallel thread, the straight edge contacts the thread crests uniformly.


**Method 2: Two diameter measurements.** Measure the major diameter at two points approximately 15mm apart along the thread axis. If the measurements differ by 0.3mm or more, the thread is tapered. If they are the same (within 0.05mm), it is parallel.


**NPT** is always tapered. **BSPT (R thread)** is always tapered. **BSPP (G thread)** is always parallel. **Metric** is always parallel (in standard form).


## Step 4: Cross-reference


You now have three values: major diameter, pitch, and taper/parallel. Enter these into the[thread cross-reference tool](https://www.rastro.ai/tools/thread-cross-reference) to identify the thread standard.


**Worked example 1: Cable gland**


Measurements:


- Major diameter: 20.0mm
- Pitch: 1.5mm (metric gauge match)
- Parallel (no taper)


Cross-reference: 20mm, 1.5mm pitch, parallel = **M20x1.5**


This is the most common metric cable gland thread in European electrical installations.


**Worked example 2: Brass fitting**


Measurements:


- Major diameter: 20.9mm
- Pitch: 14 TPI (inch gauge match)
- Parallel (no taper)


Cross-reference: ~20.95mm, 14 TPI, parallel = **G1/2 (BSPP 1/2")**


This is a British Standard Pipe Parallel thread, commonly used in plumbing and hydraulic fittings.


**Worked example 3: Steel pipe nipple**


Measurements:


- Major diameter: 21.3mm (at gauge plane)
- Pitch: 14 TPI
- Tapered (diameter reduces toward end)


Cross-reference: ~21.34mm, 14 TPI, tapered = **1/2" NPT**


This is a National Pipe Thread, standard in North American plumbing.


## Step 5: Verify


Measurement identification gets you to a likely answer. Verification confirms it.


**Go/no-go gauge.** Thread plug gauges (for female threads) and ring gauges (for male threads) give a definitive answer. The "go" gauge should enter the thread smoothly. The "no-go" gauge should not enter more than two turns.


**Test mate.** If you have a known fitting of the identified thread type, try mating them. A correct identification produces smooth engagement with no cross-threading or binding.


**Thread sealant test.** For tapered threads, apply PTFE tape and hand-tighten into a known fitting. If the thread engages correctly and seals under low pressure, the identification is likely correct.


## Ambiguous cases


Some diameter/pitch combinations are dangerously close:


**1/2" NPT vs 1/2" BSP:** Both have 14 TPI. Diameter difference is 0.39mm. If your calipers are not accurate enough, you cannot distinguish them by diameter alone. The taper check helps: NPT is always tapered. BSPP is parallel.


**M12x1.75 vs 1/2" UNF (20 TPI):** The diameters (12mm vs 12.7mm) are 0.7mm apart. Easy to measure. But a worn or damaged thread can blur the distinction.


**BSPT vs NPT at the same nominal size:** Both taper at 1:16. Both have 14 TPI at 1/2". The diameter difference (21.34mm vs 20.95mm) is the distinguishing factor. And the thread angle (60 degrees NPT vs 55 degrees BSP), which requires a thread profile gauge to measure.


When measurements are ambiguous, use a thread gauge set for the final determination. The physical engagement of a calibrated gauge is more reliable than caliper measurements on worn threads.


## Entering the result in your catalog


Once identified, record:


Field Example value


Thread standard ISO 228 (BSPP)


Thread designation G1/2


Major diameter 20.95mm


Pitch 14 TPI (1.814mm)


Thread type Parallel


Thread angle 55 degrees


For the comparison of all three systems, see[NPT vs BSP vs Metric threads](https://www.rastro.ai/resources/npt-vs-bsp-vs-metric-threads) .
